Market Overview

🌎 SpaceX Stumbles on Merger Jitters While the Rest of the Sector Splits the Week

This was the week the space sector found out it has political beta. The November 3 U.S. midterm elections delivered a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate, and a string of Elon Musk backed Texas candidates lost races Musk had personally funded to the tune of hundreds of millions of dollars. SpaceX and Tesla, the two stocks most tied to Musk's personal political brand, sold off hard into the close of the week, with SpaceX briefly trading below its June IPO price for the first time since August. By Friday the sector had mostly bought the dip, Donald Harrison quietly stepped down from SpaceX's board after eleven years, and AST SpaceMobile and Firefly Aerospace used the volatility as cover to announce one of the year's more unusual strategic bets: AST building its own rocket.
Underneath the election story, this was also a heavy earnings week. MDA Space and BlackSky both beat and raised. Redwire and Globalstar both missed and sold off. Viasat missed on the bottom line even as its defense segment kept growing. The split is a useful read on where real demand sits in this group right now: government and defense facing hardware, versus consumer facing connectivity still working through a tougher revenue environment.


SpaceX (SPCX)
SpaceX was the week's dominant story, for reasons that had little to do with rockets. Early results on election night, November 3 into November 4, pointed to a Democratic sweep, and SpaceX shares fell alongside Tesla in after hours trading as investors absorbed the result: Democrats won control of both the House and Senate, and in Texas, where Musk personally spent roughly $224 million backing Republican candidates, both Ken Paxton's Senate bid and Greg Abbott's reelection as governor went to Democratic challengers. Musk's America PAC had lost 29 of 44 federal races it backed as of Wednesday morning, November 4, against just 3 wins, per FEC filings reviewed by TheNextWeb. Outlets differed on the exact magnitude of SpaceX's decline that day, with figures ranging from roughly 3% at the close (the New York Times) to as much as 8% intraday (Investor's Business Daily), but all agree on direction: a sharp, broad based selloff that, per Reuters reporting carried by The Standard, extended into Thursday, November 5, when SpaceX fell nearly 9% and Tesla more than 11%, putting Musk's two companies on track to lose over $380 billion in combined market value for the week. SpaceX closed that Thursday at $123.62.


Friday, November 6 brought the turn. SpaceX rallied 8.62% to close at $134.27, part of what Yahoo Finance characterized as a broader rebound in tech and space names from the post election rout; Rocket Lab gained 2% the same day while AST SpaceMobile, on its own news (below), fell 8%, a reminder that the week's moves were not uniform across the sector. SpaceX's 52 week range now stands at $104.83 to $225.64. The same Friday, SpaceX disclosed that Donald Harrison, the Alphabet corporate development executive who had sat on SpaceX's board since 2015 tied to Google's original investment, was resigning effective after notifying the company on November 4. The filing said the move was not due to any disagreement with the company; Harrison remains at Alphabet, which holds SpaceX's second largest shareholder stake after Musk and which had already booked an $8.7 billion unrealized loss on that stake in its own Q3 results in late October. Deutsche Bank's Edison Yu reiterated a Buy rating and $250 price target on SpaceX on November 6, the only confirmed sell side move dated to this week; a wider look at how badly analysts currently disagree on SpaceX's valuation runs in this week's Sentiment Signal.


On the hardware side, SpaceX VP of launch Kiko Dontchev said at an industry event on November 6 that Starship Flight 15 is now targeted for November 13, though the FAA has not yet signed off: the agency is reportedly still working through SpaceX's plan to attempt "chopstick" catches of both the Super Heavy booster and the Starship upper stage at Boca Chica. A classified Space Force Falcon 9 mission, believed to carry Starshield satellites, launched from Vandenberg on November 6. No lockup tranche unlocked this week; SpaceX's next scheduled release, 342 million shares, arrives December 8, and the most recent FINRA short interest print, from the October 15 settlement date, showed 167.3 million shares short with 1.90 days to cover. A fresher short interest figure was not available as of this issue's publication; the next FINRA print covering the October 30 settlement date was not due out until November 10.


Rocket Lab (RKLB)
Rocket Lab's Electron booster flew its 99th mission, and its 20th of 2026, on November 2–3 from Mahia, New Zealand, carrying the WADATSUMI-II SAR satellite for Japanese customer iQPS: the launch marked iQPS's tenth consecutive fully successful Electron mission, with eight more booked through 2030. The same day, two insiders sold stock under existing 10b5-1 plans: CFO Adam Spice exercised options and sold 140,157 shares for roughly $7.4 million, and director Nina Armagno sold 10,926 shares for approximately $577,000, both disclosed via Form 4 on November 2. Shares rose 2% on November 6 to $46.71, caught up in the broader sector rebound from the election selloff described above, though the stock remains down roughly 38% over the trailing month. Rocket Lab reports third quarter results on November 9, just outside this issue's window.


AST SpaceMobile (ASTS)
AST SpaceMobile had an eventful week built around one striking decision: the company announced on November 6, via an SEC filing, that it will build its own reusable rocket. The deal, worth more than $1.3 billion combined, has AST licensing engine technology from Firefly Aerospace to power a new 20 ton, reusable launch vehicle called Blacklift, capable of carrying up to five of AST's BlueBird satellites per flight, targeting a first launch in late 2028. The structure includes roughly $800 million in upfront licensing fees (split between $400 million cash and 10 to 14 million AST shares), $250 million for engines on the first three rockets, and $250 million over three years for engineering support; AST says it will keep using outside launch providers in parallel, with existing agreements covering more than 100 satellite deployments through 2027 and 2028. A public Blacklift unveiling is planned for November 12 in New York.


Earlier in the week, on November 2, AST and AT&T announced what the companies describe as likely the industry's first handoff of a live phone call between a terrestrial cellular network and a direct to device satellite network, with supporting radio and core technology from Ericsson and Nokia; the underlying test was conducted on October 21 near Granite Falls, Washington. One additional report, from German language outlet Goldesel and not independently corroborated by a second source, said AST is supporting prime contractor STR on an additional phase of a U.S. Space Force sensing technology contract disclosed around November 5; no contract value was given. Shares fell 8% on November 6, to $27.76, even as SpaceX and Rocket Lab rose the same day, a divergence Yahoo Finance's roundup did not explain.


Intuitive Machines (LUNR)
Intuitive Machines picked up its third NASA award in six months on November 3, when the company was selected by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory to provide the spacecraft platform and system level integration for FALCON-RADAR, a W-band cloud profiling radar Earth science mission targeted to launch no earlier than 2029; financial terms were not disclosed. The stock was volatile all week: shares were up about 7% intraday on the FALCON-RADAR news after a two session slide that had erased more than 16% of their value, then fell 13.19% to close at $8.62 on November 5, then jumped 21.46% to close at $10.47 on November 6, without a confirmed news catalyst for either single day move. The stock remains down roughly 42% year to date. Intuitive Machines reports third quarter results on November 12.


Virgin Galactic (SPCE)
Virgin Galactic announced a three year collaboration with the nonprofit Space for Humanity on November 5, committing to fly three dedicated charter spaceflights carrying up to 18 of the group's astronauts across six seat cabins, with one or more seats on each flight potentially swapped for a research payload rack; Chief Growth Officer Megan Prichard represented the company in the announcement. Shares jumped 16.39% on November 6 to close at $2.77, though no specific news catalyst for the move could be confirmed; the company's newly unveiled Delta class spaceplane, Apeiron, remains in ground testing at Spaceport America ahead of a commercial service target that has slipped to early in the second quarter of 2027. Virgin Galactic reports third quarter results on November 12.


Redwire (RDW)
Redwire's third quarter results, released November 4, told a split story: revenue of $109.0 million missed Street estimates of roughly $135.8 million and was up only 5.4% year over year, but gross margin hit a record 32.3%, and the backlog climbed to $619.7 million, up about 75% from $411.2 million a year earlier, on $188.7 million of in quarter bookings and a 1.73 times book to bill ratio. Full year revenue guidance was reaffirmed, not raised, at $450 million to $500 million, a distinction worth noting given the backlog strength; the accompanying 10-Q also disclosed a material weakness in internal controls over financial reporting and flagged ongoing NYSE continued listing risk. Shares fell roughly 20% on November 5 as the market focused on the revenue miss over the margin and backlog improvement, per Motley Fool's same day coverage. Separately, Redwire disclosed a $20 million DARPA contract for a scaled precursor flight test of its SabreSat spacecraft under the agency's Otter very low Earth orbit program, targeting a launch in late 2027; the award follows a $44 million Phase 2 Otter contract Redwire won in November 2025. No specific analyst price target change tied to this week's earnings could be confirmed in time for publication.


Viasat (VSAT)
Viasat's fiscal second quarter results, released after market close on November 5, showed revenue of $1.2 billion, up 3% year over year on 20% growth in Defense and Advanced Technologies that offset a 3% decline in Communication Services to $815 million. The net loss widened to $129 million from $61 million a year earlier, a miss against a consensus loss estimate of roughly $0.42 per share, even as free cash flow grew 14% to $78 million and backlog rose 7% to $4.2 billion. Management now guides fiscal 2027 adjusted EBITDA to "approximately flat," a step down from previously implied growth, with free cash flow guided above $225 million and capex at $850 million to $900 million; executives flagged that recent airline customer announcements could affect 15% to 20% of aviation revenue over time. Raymond James cut its price target to $95 from $107 on November 6 while keeping an Outperform rating, citing a more conservative view on Communication Services and continued uncertainty around the timing of Viasat's strategic review; the note pointed out shares were down 22.9% over the prior week heading into that call. The stock bounced 7.70% on November 6 to close at $63.95. Separately, on November 3 Viasat's board adopted a new long term incentive program tied to the company's 40th anniversary, granting up to 2.8 million performance based RSUs with vesting hurdles between $150 and $300 against a November 2 reference price of $74.11; several executives, including SVP Craig Miller and CEO Mark Dankberg, filed Form 4 stock sales on November 4 and 5 under existing trading plans.


MDA Space (MDA.TO)
MDA Space's third quarter results, released November 5, were a clean beat and raise. Revenue (all figures in Canadian dollars) rose 21.5% year over year to C$498.1 million, led by Satellite Systems, up 26.4% to C$358.3 million on Telesat Lightspeed program volume, with Robotics and Space Operations up 2.0% to C$79.9 million on the Canadarm3 program and Geointelligence up 24.8% to C$59.9 million. Adjusted EBITDA rose 15.9% to C$96.0 million and the company swung to a C$1,328.0 million net cash position from net debt of C$120.0 million a year earlier, helped by its NYSE listing proceeds, a July bought deal offering, and a US$600 million senior notes sale completed in August. Management raised full year revenue guidance to C$1.90 billion to C$1.95 billion, from C$1.8 billion to C$1.9 billion, and adjusted EBITDA guidance to C$355 million to C$375 million. CEO Mike Greenley pointed to the successful deployment of MDA built Globalstar low Earth orbit satellites, a newly operational high volume manufacturing facility, and two new product lines, MDA MIDNIGHT and MDA AURORA BLACK, as drivers. Separately, Czechoslovak Group affiliate CSG Space filed an amended ownership disclosure on November 3 and 4 reaffirming its 9.5% stake, or 15,356,219 shares, first disclosed in mid October; the filing did not indicate any change in position size. Shares closed November 5 at $40.16, up $2.68 on the day. No confirmed post earnings analyst price target change was available in time for publication.


Planet Labs (PL)
Planet Labs released first light imagery on November 4 from Pelican-12, its newest Gen-2 high resolution satellite, captured over Luanda, Angola on October 30 following the satellite's October 20 launch on SpaceX's Bandwagon-5 rideshare mission. Pelican-12 is Planet's 25th satellite launched in 2026 across four separate launches and its first satellite capable of 30 centimeter class imagery, and it carries an Nvidia Jetson edge compute payload; Chief Space Officer James Mason represented the company in the release. Separately, a routine 13F filing disclosed that Mirae Asset Global Investments took a new stake of 2,088,886 shares, worth roughly $34.2 million, as of the September 30 reporting period. Shares traded down across multiple sessions this week, falling as much as 10% on individual days, in what commentary attributed to broad space sector weakness and valuation concerns rather than any single company specific catalyst. Planet's next earnings report is not due until early December.


Globalstar (GSAT)
Globalstar shares touched a fresh 52 week high of roughly $84.85 on November 4, just ahead of third quarter results released November 5 that showed revenue of $70.9 million, down from $73.8 million a year earlier, and a loss of $0.14 per share that missed a consensus estimate of roughly $0.12, alongside adjusted EBITDA of $30.3 million, down from $37.6 million. The results reaffirmed that Amazon's pending acquisition of Globalstar, a deal valued at roughly $11.5 billion at $90 per share in cash or stock and cleared by the FCC on October 27, remains on track to close in 2027. Shares pulled back modestly after the print to around $83.50 to $84.30. In a more unusual move, Globalstar petitioned the FCC on November 4 to scrutinize a potential conflict of interest involving Rocket Lab, which builds 17 satellite platforms for Globalstar's constellation as a subcontractor to prime contractor MDA Space; Globalstar's filing, reported by trade outlet Via Satellite and not independently corroborated elsewhere, argues Rocket Lab's pending $8 billion acquisition of satellite rival Iridium could create conflicting incentives for a company that also builds hardware for Globalstar's network.


Firefly Aerospace (FLY)
Firefly Aerospace had its highest profile week since its 2025 IPO. Two sell side price target cuts arrived early in the week, from KeyBanc on November 2 (to $35 from $50, Overweight maintained) and B. Riley on November 4 (to $40 from $50, Buy maintained), both framed as part of broader trims across space and defense technology coverage tied to multiple compression and budget uncertainty rather than anything specific to Firefly; B. Riley flagged Firefly's November 10 earnings date and a possible NASA CLPS 2.0 contract award around November 7 as near term catalysts. The bigger news came on November 6, when Firefly signed an engine supply and licensing deal worth more than $1.3 billion with AST SpaceMobile, providing 27 Miranda and 9 vacuum variant Vira engines for AST's new Blacklift rocket along with a license allowing AST to manufacture the engines itself at a new U.S. facility (full deal terms are described in AST's section above). Firefly shares surged on the news, closing November 6 up 36.8% at $20.76 from a prior close of $15.18. On November 7, Firefly said it had been onboarded as a vendor under NASA's $10 billion Commercial Lunar Payload Services 2 contract vehicle, a 10 year vendor pool rather than a specific dollar award; no task order value has been disclosed. Firefly reports third quarter results on November 10.


BlackSky Technology (BKSY)
BlackSky's third quarter results, disclosed November 5, were a record quarter and a second guidance raise this year: revenue of $42.8 million was up 118% year over year and 29% sequentially, driving the company to net income of $18.5 million, versus a net loss of $15.3 million a year earlier, and a record adjusted EBITDA margin of 29.9%. Diluted earnings per share of $0.10 beat a consensus estimate near a loss of $0.22 to $0.35. Management raised full year revenue guidance to $140 million to $150 million and adjusted EBITDA guidance to $18 million to $24 million, citing a run of contract wins including exclusive provider status under a $1 billion France and UAE backed consortium investment in a planned 50 satellite constellation, a completed assured Gen-3 imagery pilot with the U.S. government, and an expanded Gen-3 subscription with an unnamed international defense customer. Shares rose 11.56% on November 6 to close at $21.33. Separately, BlackSky announced on November 3 that it will hold an investor day on December 2 in New York. Clear Street reportedly raised its price target to $42 from $41 with a Buy rating sometime this week, though the exact date could not be confirmed in time for publication.


Takeaway
The headline story this week was political, not technical: a Democratic sweep and the apparent failure of Elon Musk's roughly half billion dollar midterm spending push hit SpaceX and Tesla hard, erased a board seat tied to Alphabet's original investment in SpaceX, and reopened questions about the pace of any eventual Tesla-SpaceX combination, even as cooler heads and a run of fresh capital bought the dip by Friday. Underneath that noise, the earnings tape split cleanly: government and defense facing hardware builders (MDA, BlackSky) beat and raised, consumer and commercial connectivity names (Viasat, Globalstar, and to a lesser extent Redwire) missed. The most interesting strategic development, AST SpaceMobile's move to build its own rocket with Firefly's engines, is a bet that launch access, not satellite technology, is now the scarcer resource in low Earth orbit. Next week brings a dense earnings slate (Rocket Lab on November 9, Firefly and Spire Global on November 10, Intuitive Machines and Virgin Galactic on November 12), AST's Blacklift unveiling on November 12, and, FAA permitting, Starship's 15th flight test on November 13.

🎯SPACEX'S POLITICAL BETA: HOW A BLUE WAVE REPRICED A TRILLION DOLLAR ROCKET COMPANY

SpaceX has been a public company for less than five months, and this week it learned something most newly listed companies never have to learn in public: that it now trades, in part, on the political fortunes of its largest shareholder. The result was the most volatile week of SpaceX's short life as a stock, and a useful case study in how a single name's governance, ownership structure, and controlling shareholder's personal brand can become a genuine, quantifiable risk factor.


The night the trade went wrong. Elon Musk spent heavily on the 2026 midterms, an estimated $446 million to $474 million across outlets including Business Insider, CNBC, and Axios, with roughly $224 million of that concentrated in Texas races alone. The bet did not pay off. As results rolled in late on November 3 and into November 4, Democrats took control of both the House and Senate, and in Texas, Musk backed candidates lost the Senate race, the governor's race, and down ballot contests for lieutenant governor and attorney general. Per FEC filings reviewed by TheNextWeb, Musk's America PAC had lost 29 of 44 federal races it funded by Wednesday morning, with roughly 93% of its spending going to races it ultimately lost. SpaceX and Tesla, the two companies whose valuations are most closely tied to Musk's personal standing, fell together in after hours trading that night.

A volatile 72 hours. What followed was genuinely hard to pin down to a single number, and worth being honest about rather than forcing a false precision. Different outlets measured SpaceX's November 4 decline anywhere from roughly 3% at the close (The New York Times) to as much as 8% intraday (Investor's Business Daily), with Yahoo Finance and Dow Jones Newswires both landing closer to 4% to 5%. All of them agree on direction and rough order of magnitude; none of them agree on the exact figure, because they were measuring different windows of the same volatile session. Reuters, carried by The Standard, reported that losses extended into November 5, with SpaceX down nearly 9% and Tesla down more than 11% that day, putting the two companies on track to lose more than $380 billion in combined market value for the week. SpaceX bottomed at a $123.62 close that Thursday before rebounding 8.62% on Friday, November 6, to close at $134.27, a swing of more than $10 a share in a single session for a company valued near $1.9 trillion.


Alphabet already felt it, and so did its board seat. The mechanics of this risk were already visible before this week even started. When Alphabet reported its own third quarter results in late October, CFO Anat Ashkenazi disclosed an $8.7 billion unrealized loss on Alphabet's SpaceX equity stake, cutting Alphabet's diluted earnings per share by $0.55, attributed to SpaceX's share price falling roughly 11.7% during the quarter. This week's aftershock came on November 6, when SpaceX disclosed that Donald Harrison, the Alphabet corporate development executive who had held a board seat tied to Google's original investment since 2015, was resigning, effective after he notified the company on November 4. SpaceX's filing said the departure was not the result of any disagreement, and Harrison remains at Alphabet. But the timing, two days after a swing that wiped tens of billions off Alphabet's own SpaceX mark, invites an obvious question about whether a large strategic shareholder wants a board seat tied to a stock this volatile and this exposed to one man's politics.


The merger premium now carries a political discount. SpaceX's valuation has never traded purely on launch cadence or Starlink subscriber growth; a meaningful part of the bull case since the IPO has rested on persistent speculation about an eventual combination with Tesla, with Bloomberg reporting in late October on a potential deal structure valuing the combined entity near $3.7 trillion and a possible announcement in the first half of 2027. This week's results complicate that story. Dan Ives of Yorkville, quoted November 4, argued that Democratic control could slow the pace of AI linked data center construction in Texas, a state central to both companies' expansion plans, and that "SpaceX and Musk are clearly caught front and center in this spiderweb." Gary Black of The Future Fund separately warned that political backlash of this kind is exactly the sort of event that compresses arbitrage premiums in speculative merger trades. Neither company has confirmed a deal is imminent, but the market's working assumption, that a Musk backed combination carries some embedded premium, just got a live demonstration of the downside case.


Analysts can't agree on the number, and that disagreement is the real signal. Strip away the week's drama and look at where sell side analysts actually sit on SpaceX, and the dispersion is extraordinary for a company this large. As of late October, individual 12 month price targets ranged from Piper Sandler's $140 at the low end to Raymond James' $800 at the high end, a more than five fold spread, with J.P. Morgan's Doug Anmuth raising his target to $500 on October 21 citing a path to $175 billion in 2027 revenue, while KeyBanc sat at Hold the same week. A consensus average near $255, which is where the Street sits this week per StockAnalysis.com's 40 analyst panel, flattens that disagreement into a single deceptively tidy number. The reality is that nobody has a confident model for what SpaceX is worth, because nobody has a confident model for how much of its value depends on Musk himself, how a Tesla combination would be priced, or how exposed the stock now is to political and regulatory sentiment that has nothing to do with Starship test flights or Starlink subscriber counts.


What to watch next. The next concrete catalyst tied purely to SpaceX's share structure is the December 8 lockup unlock, when 342 million shares become eligible for sale, a release that will land into whatever political and valuation environment exists five weeks from now. On the operating side, Starship Flight 15 is targeted for November 13, pending FAA sign off on SpaceX's plan to attempt double booster and upper stage catches at Boca Chica; a clean flight would give the bulls a fundamentals story to point to again. The lockup calendar and every subsequent tranche are tracked in full at Orbit Alpha's lockup calendar.


Takeaway. SpaceX spent its first five months as a public company proving it could execute operationally while posting its first profitable quarter. It spent this week proving something less comfortable for holders: that its stock now carries a genuine, hard to model political risk premium tied directly to its controlling shareholder, one that can move tens of billions of dollars in market value in a single session independent of anything the rockets themselves do. Until that changes, or until the market develops more confidence in where a Tesla combination and Musk's political standing actually settle, expect SpaceX to keep trading with a volatility profile that looks more like an event driven special situation than a $1.9 trillion aerospace company's usual rhythm.
